item.title: Air alert sounds hours after attack on Russia-bound ship in the Gulf of Finland
item.description:
Air alert sounds hours after attack on Russia-bound ship in the Gulf of Finland
The governor of Kaliningrad says a rare air alert sounded in the Russian exclave near Poland and LithuaniaByThe Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:14 AM
Share
KYIV, Ukraine -- A rare air alert sounded in Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave near Poland and Lithuania, according to the local governor, as claims circulated online of drone activity near a major naval base there.
The alert late Saturday in Kaliningrad came hours after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland set fire to a Russian cargo ship bound for the region, which is a key base for Russia's Baltic Fleet. Finnish emergency services were still working to extinguish the blaze on Sunday.
Photos and video posted online show drone activity around the city of Baltiysk, where much of the fleet is stationed. But The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify the authenticity of the images.
According to local media, air raid sirens were heard in Kaliningrad for the first time since Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
The Kaliningrad governor, Alexei Bezprozvannykh, said that “a suspicious object coming from the direction of Lithuania” triggered the alert in the Nemansky district near the Lithuanian border, about 170 kilometers (105 miles) northeast of Baltiysk.
On Russian Telegram channels, posts by users saying they were Baltiysk residents described air defenses working there during the night. They featured photos and videos of bright streaks against the night sky, with crackling sounds heard in the background.
Kaliningrad authorities on Sunday denounced as fake one photo, supposedly from Baltiysk, that showed clouds of smoke rising into the night sky, while an orange haze glowed on the horizon. They told Russian state media that the photo “had nothing to do with the region.”
As of Sunday morning, Russian authorities reported no casualties or damage in Kaliningrad.

item.title: Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
item.description:
Okinawa celebrates restored Shuri Castle hall 7 years after fire
Officials and residents in Okinawa have celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall, marking a significant return of the island's cultural symbolByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:13 AM
Share
TOKYO -- Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on Sunday, its deep red exterior and dragon ornaments marking the return of a symbol of the island's heritage seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.
The fire on Oct. 31, 2019, destroyed several buildings at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa’s prefectural capital, as it was hosting a festival. Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread from building to building in strong winds. Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.
“The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said at Sunday’s ceremony in the courtyard outside the main hall. "Seven years after the major loss, as we mark this milestone of the main hall restoration, I am deeply moved and delighted.”
The castle is a symbol of Okinawa’s cultural heritage dating to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which lasted about 450 years from 1429 until 1879, when Japan annexed the island.
It also represents Okinawa’s recovery from World War II. The castle burned down in 1945 during the Battle of Okinawa, which killed about 200,000 people, many of them civilians.
Koja thanked historians, artisans and other experts from across Japan who contributed to the restoration, as well as donors at home and abroad. He called for rebuilding the rest of the castle, saying the opening of the main hall, known as Seiden, is "not the end.”
The 2019 fire destroyed Seiden and two adjacent halls, as well as four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.

item.title: What to know about tear gas and reproductive health, as concerns are raised in France
item.description:
What to know about tear gas and reproductive health, as concerns are raised in France
French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent protests that police stop using tear gas because of rising concerns about menstrual changes and reproductive health issuesBySYLVIE CORBET Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 7:07 AM
Share
PARIS -- French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection.
The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons.
Here’s what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health.
Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it.
Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches.
Mélina Galland, 24, was working as an independent photographer during Oct. 17 protests in Paris that were marred by rioting and looting. She wore a double surgical mask along with a diving mask when tear gas grenades were fired.

item.title: In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
item.description:
In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
As the winter cold sets in, Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities face a growing shortage of window installers as Russian attacks leave homes shattered and families exposed to the coldByDMYTRO ZHYHINAS Associated Press and DEREK GATOPOULOS Associated PressNovember 22, 2026, 12:00 AM
KYIV, Ukraine -- For weeks after a missile exploded in front of her apartment block, Oleksandra Horban found pieces of glass in her small apartment.
She threw out her 2-year-old son’s plush toys which were covered with glass shards. Outside her ground-floor home, mangled window frames were piled onto a mountain of debris awaiting removal. Pieces of glass were mixed with autumn leaves on the muddy ground.
“Even now we still find glass,” Horban said. “If we vacuum three times, wash the floor and clean up, we’ll still find those microscopic pieces somewhere, in the bed or in the toys.”
As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows with Russian missile and drone attacks continuing to damage buildings, leaving residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) last winter.
Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.
Horban lives in a Soviet-era “groundscraper” - an enormous horizontal apartment block in the Ukrainian capital. A missile blast in October damaged a vertical section of apartments and shattered hundreds of facade windows.
Most shattered windows have been temporarily covered with fiberboard or tarps. Some boards have small openings fitted with Plexiglas to let daylight into apartments.
New windows in Horban’s apartment would cost about $1,700, more than three times the country’s average salary. Government compensation can take three to four months.

item.title: Fire at Indonesian candy factory leaves 3 dead and dozens of workers unaccounted for
item.description:
Fire at Indonesian candy factory leaves 3 dead and dozens of workers unaccounted for
A fire has swept through a candy factory in Indonesia’s Banten province, leaving three people dead and rescue teams searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted forByNINIEK KARMINI Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 11:14 PM
Share
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- A fire swept through a candy factory in Indonesia ’s Banten province Saturday, leaving three people dead and rescue teams searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted for, officials said.
The blaze broke out at the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia factory in Serang district, in Banten province, which borders Jakarta. The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.
The National Search and Rescue Agency released a statement saying that 15 people were rescued alive, including four injured workers. Rescue teams were still searching for the 36 unaccounted-for workers.
“The fire is still burning in several locations, and firefighting teams are continuing extinguishing and cooling operations,” said Rizky Dwianto, an operations official at the Banten Search and Rescue Agency.
He said firefighters from Serang district and Banten province were battling flames in several parts of the facility more than 12 hours after the fire began.
Television reports showed flames engulfing the three-story factory, sending thick black smoke into the sky, and causing panic among nearby residents and workers. The floor of the burned-out structure was littered with twisted metal, blackened corrugated iron roofing and other debris.

item.title: At least 24 dead in Nigeria when boat going to funeral capsizes
item.description:
At least 24 dead in Nigeria when boat going to funeral capsizes
Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to be on board.ByDYEPKAZAH SHIBAYAN Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 3:32 PM
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A boat carrying people to a funeral has capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, emergency services said on Saturday.
The boat was taking passengers from one community to another for a burial ceremony when it sank on Friday in Bayelsa State in the country’s South South region, Nigeria’s National Emergency Management Agency spokesman Manzo Ezeki said in a statement.
He said that search and rescue operations were ongoing without specifying how many people were missing.
Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said on Friday that another 24 people had been rescued and sought medical assistance.
Authorities haven't said how many passengers were believed to have been on board.
Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.

The Bayelsa state government responded by urging boat operators and passengers to adhere to safety regulations.
“Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life,” Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Boat tragedies are common in Nigeria. A lack of enforcement of safety regulations means faulty boats without life jackets sometimes operate in the country.

item.title: Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
item.description:
Taiwan warns Canada’s Carney that deeper ties with China come with risks
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has tried to deepen trade ties with China.ByROB GILLIES Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 12:39 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia -- Taiwan’s deputy foreign minister warned on Saturday that Prime Minister Mark Carney risks exposing Canada to the very economic coercion he has cautioned against by deepening trade ties with China, saying that Taiwan has learned the hard way that dependence on Beijing comes with consequences.
“We worry. We worry,” Chen Ming-chi told The Associated Press in an interview at the Halifax International Security Forum when asked about Carney’s efforts to improve relations with China.
Carney has warned that major powers are using economic integration as a weapon, citing U.S. tariffs and China’s restrictions on critical minerals. He has urged middle powers to diversify their trade relationships to avoid economic coercion.
Chen praised Carney’s speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, but questioned whether Canada should deepen ties with countries that don’t share its democratic values.
“Who do you want to choose as your partners?” he asked.
“You have your own history. You have two Michaels,” Chen said, referring to former Canadian diplomat Michael Kovrig and businessman Michael Spavor, whose ne arly three-year detention in China prompted accusations of hostage diplomacy.
The two were arrested in 2018 shortly after Canada detained Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. They were released in September 2021, the same day Meng returned to China. Beijing denied their detention was politically motivated.
Chen’s warning came days after Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and agreed to additional tariff reductions as Canada seeks to diversify trade during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

item.title: 11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of cartel leader
item.description:
11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of cartel leader
At least 11 people have been killed in a burst of violence in Mexico’s Sinaloa stateByMEGAN JANETSKY Associated Press, FABIOLA SÁNCHEZ Associated Press, and MARTÍN URISTA Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 8:23 AM
Share
GUASAVE, Mexico -- A burst of violence in Mexico’s Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after an intense firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning.
Mexico’s Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.
The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.
Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos,” a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.
Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

item.title: Black music producer's lawyer hails landmark ruling as French court finds racist police violence
item.description:
Black music producer's lawyer hails landmark ruling as French court finds racist police violence
A French court has acknowledged the racist nature of a violent incident involving police officers and sentenced them to prisonBySAMUEL PETREQUIN Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 6:37 AM
PARIS -- The lawyer for a Black man who was beaten up by three French police officers hailed a “historic ruling” on Saturday after a court acknowledged the racist nature of the violence and sentenced them to between one and two years in prison.
The assault on Michel Zecler, a music producer, took place six years ago during the coronavirus pandemic and was caught on camera. It showed the officers repeatedly punching him, using a truncheon and tear gas against him for no apparent reason.
Zecler told The Associated Press after the incident that the officers hurled repeated insults at him, including a very strong racist epithet.
“What is very important is that the racist nature of the violence he suffered has been recognized," Zecler's lawyer, Serge Money, told France Info. “As a legal professional, one can only be satisfied. This is a first.”
Money said that from the very beginning of the proceedings, Zecler maintained that he had been racially insulted, whereas the defendants’ accounts were somewhat inconsistent.
"Ultimately, they were convicted of lying, as the falsification of written records was established,” he said. The verdict was issued late Friday in Paris.
Videos published showed the violent arrest of Zecler in the 17th arrondissement of the French capital. The three officers intended to stop him for not wearing a face mask during the restrictions imposed because of the pandemic.
The video images, obtained by the AP, both from a security camera inside the studio and filmed by neighbors outside, showed officers following Zecler inside his music studio, where they could be seen repeatedly punching him and beating him with a truncheon.

item.title: Missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
item.description:
Missile attack on Zelenskyy's hometown in central Ukraine kills 2 and wounds scores
A Russian strike on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, has killed two people and wounded 60 othersBySAMYA KULLAB Associated Press and ELISE MORTON Associated PressNovember 21, 2026, 5:55 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- A Russian strike on the center of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.
A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on the city in central Ukraine, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.
The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said.
The attack fits the pattern of Moscow’s heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to illegally annexed Crimea.
The missile attack came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.
European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.
